title: Liberté: la poesia caduta dal cielo
description: Paul Éluard la scrisse come una poesia d'amore e la trasformò in un grido di resistenza. Nel 1942 la RAF la lanciò sulla Francia occupata. Storia di una poesia che ha viaggiato più di qualunque soldato.
contents:
Ci sono poesie che si leggono e poesie che si attraversano. Liberté di Paul Éluard appartiene alla seconda specie: ventuno strofe che camminano, una dopo l’altra, sempre con lo stesso passo, finché all’ultima riga non capisci dove ti hanno portato.
Una poesia d’amore che cambiò destinatario
Éluard la scrisse durante l’occupazione tedesca della Francia. Il titolo originale era Une seule pensée, “un solo pensiero”, e il progetto era semplice: un lungo elenco di luoghi su cui il poeta scrive un nome, fino a rivelare alla fine quello della donna amata. Per Éluard quella donna era Nusch, sua moglie.
Strada facendo, però, si accorse che la parola che aveva in testa era un’altra. Nella Francia del 1941 e del 1942 c’era un desiderio più grande di qualunque amore privato, condiviso da tutti quelli che vivevano sotto l’occupazione. Così l’ultima parola della poesia diventò Liberté, e la poesia d’amore diventò una poesia per tutti.
Come è fatta
La struttura è la sua forza. Sono ventuno quartine costruite tutte allo stesso modo: tre versi che nominano una superficie su cui scrivere e un quarto verso che ritorna identico, come un ritornello. È un’anafora ostinata, quasi una preghiera.
Le superfici cambiano e raccontano una vita intera. Si parte dai quaderni e dal banco di scuola, si passa alla natura (gli alberi, la sabbia, la neve, il mare), poi alla città, alla casa, al corpo dell’amata, e infine ai luoghi più fragili: la stanchezza, l’assenza, la solitudine, la morte stessa. Il nome viene scritto ovunque, anche dove sembrerebbe impossibile. È il modo di Éluard di dire che la libertà non è un’idea astratta: si scrive su ogni cosa che tocchiamo.
Solo nell’ultima strofa la parola arriva, come una porta che si apre in fondo a un lungo corridoio.
Il viaggio clandestino
La poesia uscì il 3 aprile 1942 nella raccolta Poésie et vérité 1942, stampata clandestinamente dalle edizioni de la Main à plume. A giugno Max-Pol Fouchet la ripubblicò nella rivista Fontaine, che usciva ad Algeri, perché arrivasse anche nella zona non occupata.
Poi accadde la cosa più straordinaria. A Londra la ristampò La France libre, la rivista della Francia di de Gaulle, e la Royal Air Force ne lanciò migliaia di copie con il paracadute sulla Francia occupata. Alcune arrivarono ai partigiani del maquis insieme alle casse di armi. Una poesia era diventata, letteralmente, un rifornimento.
La musica
Nel 1943 Francis Poulenc mise in musica Liberté insieme ad altre sette poesie di Éluard nella cantata Figure humaine, per doppio coro misto a dodici voci. Scritta sotto l’occupazione, in Francia non poteva essere eseguita: la prima esecuzione avvenne alla radio della BBC, in inglese, il 25 marzo 1945.
Perché leggerla oggi
Liberté si impara a memoria facilmente, ed è per questo che ha viaggiato tanto: nelle scuole francesi, sui muri, sui cartelli delle manifestazioni. Ma la sua lezione più bella sta nella forma. Ripetere lo stesso gesto ventuno volte, su ventuno superfici diverse, è un esercizio di pazienza e di ostinazione. La libertà, dice Éluard, non si conquista una volta sola: si scrive ogni giorno, su tutto.
Il testo integrale si trova facilmente nelle antologie di Éluard e online; per la storia della poesia, una buona sintesi è la voce di Wikipedia.

title: Capoliveri: A beautiful village in Elba
description: Elba is the biggest island of the Tuscany Archipelago. Capoliveri is a small town of the island that deserves a stop. Despite being a very characteristic italian village, there are famous beaches around (like l'Innamorata) and natural landscapes.
contents:
The small town of Capoliveri is perched on a hill 167 meters above sea level, on the slopes of Monte Calmita. In the past, it was tied to agricultural and mining activities, but today it is one of the most characteristic and lively centers on Elba Island, rich in charm and history.
Characterized by a very particular architecture, the town still retains the appearance of a medieval village with its narrow and picturesque arcaded alleys called “chiassi,” which hide small artisan shops and charming eateries where you can enjoy a typical dish or a good glass of wine. There is indeed a restaurat called “Il chiasso” exactly because the tables to eat are in the small stairs of the alley.
Curiosity: There have always been several hypotheses about the meaning of the name and the origins of the town. Caput Liberum, meaning “sacred to Liber,” better known as Bacchus or Dionysus, might refer to a place rich in vineyards and excellent wine. Alternatively, it could more likely derive from the very shape of the section of the island where Capoliveri is located: free, as it is surrounded by the sea.
Capoliveri is divided into four distinct districts: Il Fosso, La Torre, La Fortezza, and Il Baluardo, which compete every October during the traditional Festa dell’Uva (Grape Festival), staging extraordinary choreographies on various harvest-related themes.
The Festa dell’Uva is not the only cultural highlight in Capoliveri. On July 14, the Festa dell’Innamorata is celebrated, inspired by an ancient legend of two young lovers, Lorenzo and Maria.


Capoliveri, Spiaggia dell’innamorata Luglio 14.



This traditional celebration dates back to the second half of the 17th century when Don Domingo Cardenas
A fallen nobleman of Spanish origin settled in Innamorata, then called Cala de lo Ferro, and recounted the events of an ancient legend passed down among the fishermen. It is the story of Lorenzo and Maria, two young lovers whose relationship was hindered by their families and social differences. The two lovers had made this corner of paradise, known as the Beach of the Innamorata, their love refuge. But one day, pirates captured Lorenzo and threw his body into the sea before Maria’s eyes. Overcome with despair, Maria threw herself into the waters, vanishing forever into the depths of the sea, leaving behind only the shawl she had been wearing.
This symbolic celebration in Capoliveri and on the Island of Elba has grown in prominence over time, attracting attention from both national and international media.
Every year, the same magical ritual takes place: at 8:30 PM, a thousand candles are lit in the bay of Innamorata. At 9:15 PM, the bells of Capoliveri’s church announce the Historical Parade in period costumes, which begins in the town’s historic center and proceeds on foot to the enchanting beach of Innamorata. “Maria,” the girl from the legend who is said to have thrown herself into the sea to follow “Lorenzo,” her beloved taken by the Saracens, dives from the Ciarpa rock into the sea, letting her white shawl (the Ciarpa) fall. Immediately afterward, the “Challenge of the Ciarpa” begins: four rowing boats, representing the four districts of Capoliveri’s castle – the “Baluardo,” the “Fosso,” the “Torre,” and the “Fortezza” – compete to capture the Ciarpa.
The entire coast is exceptionally beautiful, characterized by countless coves and small bays wrapped in the unmistakable beauty and scent of Mediterranean vegetation. Examples include the inlets of Morcone, Pareti, and Innamorata, once small fishing villages and now popular vacation spots, as well as the serene beaches of Naregno, Madonna delle Grazie, Felciaio, Norsi, or the larger and busier beaches of Lacona, Lido, and Margidore.
As small as it may seems, this town is perfect to stay in a quiet place, be creative and enjoy a peaceful mind. There is a special corner among the streets and glimpses of Capoliveri, an unexpected spot discovered by descending the ancient staircase behind the town square. It is the Borgo degli Artisti (Artists’ Village), where painters, sculptors, poets, and writers come together, bringing moments of art and culture to life in the historic center perched on the hills of the Calamita promontory. The Borgo degli Artisti, as named by its curator Michelangelo Venturini, has been welcoming artists—local and beyond—since May, and will continue to do so throughout the summer, giving a platform to expressiveness and creativity. Below an image referred to the artists in general:


Caput Liberum, a creative spot.



Here an italian poetry that Franco Marelli, an italian writer, wrote for Capoliveri:


Qui a Caput Liberum si ritrova la calma, 
ed il senso delle cose piccole, eppure grandi: 
un pasto condiviso, 
una sera silenziosa, 
un soffio gentile che sfiora il viso. 
Prendilo, tienilo stretto, 
questo alito lieve, flebile, 
è ciò che ti resta 
quando la tua terra si fa ricordo, 
e il vento, lento, diventa sordo. 
Mettilo all’orecchio, 
non lasciarlo sfuggire, 
sospiraci dentro, infondigli forza. 
Poi trattienilo forte, 
perché rimanga 
sempre con te.

title: Palermo: a gem in the north-west of Sicily
description: Sicily is a wonderful land, full of passion and with incredible welcoming people. Living here is not easy, but beuaty has its own price to pay. Enjoy the mind trip!
contents:
This has been my first trip in the North-West part of Sicily. The island has a lot to offer but, given the limited amount of time, I dedicated four days at the capital of Sicily, Palermo. The first day we went to Teatro Massimo, which is the biggest lyric theater in Italy and the third in Europe after the Opèra National of Paris and the Staatsoper of Vienna. Apart from the beauty of the building, what captures the attention of a focused observed is the phrase in the theater pediment:


Teatro Massimo by night.



              L’arte rinnova i popoli e ne rivela la vita. 
              Vano delle scene il diletto ove non miri a preparar l’avvenire.
After this we proceeded to one of the main street of Palermo, Via Maqueda, which brought us to the square named “i 4 canti”. Two wonderful images of the “canti” with pictures of the fruit:


4 Canti Square by night.



4 Canti Square by night.



The Quattro Canti, properly so called, are the four decorative structures that define the space of the crossroads. Built between 1609 and 1620, and topped with (white marble) coats of arms representing the royal, senatorial, and viceroyal seals, the four façades are articulated on multiple levels, featuring decorations based on the use of architectural orders and figurative elements that, from bottom to top, follow a principle of ascension from the natural world to the heavens. The four façade levels are decorated as follows: on the lower level, fountains represent the rivers of the ancient city (Oreto, Kemonia, Pannaria, Papireto); above, a Doric order contains allegories of the four seasons (represented by Aeolus, Venus, Ceres, and Bacchus); the next order, in Ionic style, houses statues of Charles V, Philip II, Philip III, and Philip IV; finally, in the uppermost order, the four Palermitan saints—Agatha, Nympha, Olivia, and Christina—patronesses of the city before the advent of Saint Rosalia (1624) and Saint Benedict of San Fratello (1652).

title: Brazil: a cultural shock
description:
Coming to this wonderful country will change completely your point of view. Be ready to be 
in a rollercoaster, a good one!
contents:
I went to Brazil for the first time in October 2018. Differently from the usual touristic routes (Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo), I went to visit Brasilia and Goias. The former is the capital of Brazil located in the district of Brasilia and the latter is an importan state located in the center of the nation. From the beginning, I had the privilege to enjoy the richness and variety of this country in terms of nature and society. If you are interested in the dimension of Brazil compared to Europe, you can have a look at a Peters World Map.
Below you can see some of the images I took in the city of Goiás (also known as Góias Velho) which is a brazilian municipality classified as UNESCO World Heritage and ancient capital of the homonym state.


A typical house.




A church.




A clothes shop


The city is also famous to be the place of birth of the most well-known brazilian poetess named Cora Coralina. One of his famous poetry Assim eu vejo a vida:
                       A vida tem duas faces:
                       Positiva e negativa
                       O passado foi duro
                       mas deixou o seu legado
                       Saber viver é a grande sabedoria
                       Que eu possa dignificar
                       Minha condição de mulher,
                       Aceitar suas limitações
                       E me fazer pedra de segurança
                       dos valores que vão desmoronando.
                       Nasci em tempos rudes
                       Aceitei contradições
                       lutas e pedras
                       como lições de vida
                       e delas me sirvo
                       Aprendi a viver.
                       
                       
For my second trip in Brazil, I went to the south in the state of Paranà (the one with the highest Human Development Index). The beautiful image below is a Volkswagen Beetle which we can still see in the street of Morretes, which is a small historic city of the Brazilian state of Paraná.

title: On the Self-Respect
description: A beautiful text by Joan Didion, an American writer and journalist. If you search a way to understand where self-esteem comes from and the true meaning of self-respect, read this.
contents:
Once, in a dry season, I wrote in large letters across two pages of a notebook that innocence ends when one is stripped of the delusion that one likes oneself. Although now, some years later, I marvel that a mind on the outs with itself should have nonetheless made painstaking record of its every tremor, I recall with embarrassing clarity the flavor of those particular ashes. It was a matter of misplaced self-respect.
I had not been elected to Phi Beta Kappa. This failure could scarcely have been more predictable or less ambiguous (I simply did not have the grades), but I was unnerved by it; I had somehow thought myself a kind of academic Raskolnikov, curiously exempt from the cause-effect relationships that hampered others. Although the situation must have had even then the approximate tragic stature of Scott Fitzgerald’s failure to become president of the Princeton Triangle Club, the day that I did not make Phi Beta Kappa nevertheless marked the end of something, and innocence may well be the word for it. I lost the conviction that lights would always turn green for me, the pleasant certainty that those rather passive virtues which had won me approval as a child automatically guaranteed me not only Phi Beta Kappa keys but happiness, honour, and the love of a good man (preferably a cross between Humphrey Bogart in Casablanca and one of the Murchisons in a proxy fight); lost a certain touching faith in the totem power of good manners, clean hair, and proven competence on the Stanford-Binet scale. To such doubtful amulets had my self-respect been pinned, and I faced myself that day with the nonplussed wonder of someone who has come across a vampire and found no garlands of garlic at hand.
Source: https://www.vogue.com/article/joan-didion-self-respect-essay-1961

title: Il Turismo a Piombino: uno sguardo ai dati
description:
Piombino è da sempre un polo industriale, ma negli ultimi anni il turismo è cresciuto molto. Dal 2005 al 2024 i dati mostrano che la maggior parte dei turisti viene dalla Toscana, ma aumentano anche i visitatori dal Nord Italia, in particolare Lombardia, Piemonte ed Emilia-Romagna. Crescono soprattutto campeggi e agriturismi, che attirano gran parte dei turisti grazie alla loro offerta più ampia, mentre gli alloggi privati, dopo un boom fino al 2015, hanno subito un calo e non si sono più ripresi dopo il Covid. In generale, il turismo a Piombino si sta diversificando e diventando sempre più importante accanto all’industria.
Fonte: Elaborazione su dati https://www.regione.toscana.it/statistiche/banca-dati-turismo.
